title: Why Do We Shake Hands?
parts: You do it with strangers, with bosses, with people you just met.
A quick grip, a shake, and it's over.
Four different explanations claim to know why we do it.
One says it proves you're unarmed.
One says it seals a deal.
One is pure chemistry.
One says there's a cleaner way.
We'll mark every claim: documented, disputed, or myth.
By the end, you'll know which of these four explanations actually holds up.
And you'll find out what your hand picks up, and passes on, every time you shake someone else's.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
Case one: the handshake proves you carry no weapon.
It's the most repeated explanation of all.
But the very page that tells this story admits it needs a better source.
No ancient text says this is why the gesture began.
Disputed.
Case two: the handshake seals a promise.
For this one, there's an actual picture, one of the oldest we have.
Around the ninth century before our era, an Assyrian carving shows two kings clasping hands.
Shalmaneser the Third of Assyria, and Marduk-zakir-shumi the First of Babylon.
It's carved into the base of a throne found at Nimrud, now kept in the Iraq Museum.
Historians read it as a public show of alliance between the two kingdoms.
Documented as an image — the alliance is their reading of it.
And it's only "one of the earliest known" depictions, not the first ever.
Nobody can claim that title.
Myth, if anyone says otherwise.
In Greece, the same gesture, called dexiosis, appears in art from the fifth century before our era.
The word meant greeting, or hospitality.
So the gesture is tied to agreements in two separate ancient civilizations.
Documented.
But the specific idea that it began to seal an oath has no solid source of its own.
Disputed, as an origin.
Case three: it's chemistry.
In twenty fifteen, researchers at the Weizmann Institute filmed people shaking hands without telling them why.
Afterward, people touched their own hand to their face, and sniffed it, far more than before they shook hands.
The study found real chemical compounds that moved from one hand to the other during the shake.
Our reading: a handshake carries more than a greeting.
But that chemistry doesn't explain why the gesture began nearly three thousand years earlier.
Documented as an effect today — not as an origin.
Case four: there's a cleaner way.
In twenty fourteen, researchers tested the fist bump against the handshake, using a harmless lab bacteria on gloved hands.
The handshake transferred far more than the fist bump did.
It shows a custom can change when there's a reason.
It doesn't tell us why the first handshake happened.
Documented, in a glove study.
Let's count what we actually know.
The oldest picture, the chemistry, and the fist bump study: all documented.
The weapon story and the sealed oath, as origins: both disputed.
And "the first handshake in history" is still myth, if anyone claims it.
So after nearly three thousand years, nobody knows who shook hands first.
Nobody knows if it started once, or many times, in many places.
Maybe a gesture survives simply because it's cheap, quick, and easy to read as trust.
Our reading — no source says it.
The question of who started it stays open.
We draw a different shape on cards, on cakes, on cushions.
It doesn't look like a heart at all.
So why does the heart symbol look nothing like a heart?
